newsitem.title: FRANCE: France reshuffles spending to fund new measures.
newsitem.headline: France reshuffles spending to fund new measures.

text.p: France's new Socialist-led government said on Wednesday it would redirect spending plans to pay for new economic measures, including the creation of some 40,000 to 70,000 public sector jobs for young people.

Ministers said the government would scrap or reallocate 11 billion francs ($1.9 billion) in spending planned by the previous centre-right administration and spend 11.1 billion francs on the new measures.
"There is not one more franc of (budget) deficit in this decree," Finance Minister Dominique Strauss-Kahn told a news conference.
"These 11.1 billion francs will be covered either through reallocations, or through scrapping of credit lines," Christian Sautter, junior minister responsible for the budget, said.
The measures will be the first to be implemented by the government, swept to power in an upset parliamentary election on June 1 with a promise to make the fight for jobs a priority.
It has insisted, however, that it will not worsen the budget deficit and now is trying to square the circle of fulfilling campaign pledges while sticking to sound financial management.

It is awaiting the results of an audit of public finances due on July 21 before deciding whether it needs to take any action to curb the public deficit, likely to be done through new savings and higher taxes on companies and the wealthy.

Finance Ministry documents said the new measures announced on Wednesday would be financed by releasing some of the 9.8 billion francs in credits frozen by the previous conservative government in March.
Of eight billion francs frozen in the civil budget, 2.5 billion will be reallocated to pay for justice, housing, education and research.
The 1.8 billion francs in the military budget frozen in March would be scrapped altogether, the documents said.

The rest of the new spending measures would be funded by scrapping spending planned elsewhere or by reallocating spending from one area to another, meaning that out of the original money frozen in March 5.5 billion will remain so.

The new spending measures will include two billion francs to create public sector jobs for young people. "It represents several tens of thousands of jobs...at least 40,000 to 50,000 and at most 60,000 to 70,000," Strauss-Kahn said.
Many of the jobs would be in education and are expected to involve providing back-up to teachers in state schools.
Strauss-Kahn said the money for this would be reallocated from job creation programmes set up by the previous centre-right government which he argued were not effective.
A family back-to-school payment will be raised to 1,600 francs for low income families from 1,000 at a total cost of 6.4 billion francs in 1997.

The government also plans to spend 600 million francs to help low-income people find housing, 1.15 billion francs on public housing, 290 million francs on additional school lunch subsidies, and 600 million in extra spending not accounted for in the existing budget.
Separately the government also confirmed it wanted to modify a pensions fund law introduced by the previous government to change the tax treatment of company contributions to the funds.

The Socialist party had criticised the bill when it was introduced earlier this year saying that favourable tax treatment of company contributions might encourage employers to put money into the private funds rather than into wages.
That would put the universal pay-as-you-go pension system at a disadvantage since it is paid for out of payroll taxes.
Strauss-Kahn said on Tuesday he would hold early talks with interested parties to modify the pension funds law. ($ = 5.942 French Francs)
